newsitem.title: FINLAND: FINNISH SELIN FINANCE SAYS STILL SEEKING PARTNER.
newsitem.headline: FINNISH SELIN FINANCE SAYS STILL SEEKING PARTNER.

text.p: Finnish brokerage house Selin Finance Oy will look for another partner after merger talks with Aktia Bank ended without agreement, Selin's main owner and chairman Carolus Rosenlew said on Wednesday.
"It does not end here. We are looking for other cooperation partners," Rosenlew told Reuters by telephone.
Selin and Aktia said late on Tuesday that talks on Aktia buying Selin, which started on February 3, had ended without agreement.
Rosenlew said Selin was open to all options.
"We could be looking at a strategic alliance, co-ownership could come into consideration, no doors have been closed," he said, but declined comment on potential partner candidates.

For Selin, the chief aim was to find a structure that would help it adapt to changes ahead on the financial services markets, Rosenlew said. "We need to strengthen our positions ... to raise our profile," he said.
In 1996, Selin's net profit was about 2.7 million markka, down on 1995, he said, adding revenue had been largely unchanged while costs had risen "perhaps too much".

Selin Finance managing director Juhani Elomaa said the 1996 earnings were "satisfactory" with the decline in profit mainly due to lower commissions. He said there were "certain pressures" for a further decline.

In the near future, the most significant growth segment would be financial and investment services for private investors, Elomaa said. The trend was also towards more proprietary trading, which would underline the importace of a strong balance sheet, he said.
Rosenlew agreed, saying this was a strategic factor behind Selin's quest for a partner.

"Trading on the bourse has changed ... most of our competitors are trading through their own portfolios and this requires a lot of capital, which I, as a private individual, don't have the capacity to mobilise," he said.
Echoing Rosenlew, Elomaa said the ability to offer services to private investors would be crucial for success.
"Every house that does not have its own distribution network or is not part of an international group will have to take a close look at its strategy," he said.
Elomaa expected trading and investment services to be gradually polarised with "niche players" on the one hand and "mega houses" on the other.
